WITH consumed AS (                    -- each partition a group consumes, from its first commit
  SELECT c.group_id, c.topic, c.partition_id, MIN(s.taken_at) AS first_at
  FROM committed_offsets c
  JOIN snapshots s USING (snapshot_id)
  GROUP BY c.group_id, c.topic, c.partition_id
), grid AS (                          -- every snapshot from that first commit on
  SELECT g.group_id, g.topic, g.partition_id, s.snapshot_id, s.taken_at
  FROM consumed g
  JOIN snapshots s ON s.taken_at >= g.first_at
), lags AS (
  SELECT gr.group_id, gr.taken_at,
         GREATEST(l.log_end_offset - (
           SELECT c.committed_offset            -- latest commit at or before this snapshot
           FROM committed_offsets c
           JOIN snapshots s2 USING (snapshot_id)
           WHERE c.group_id = gr.group_id AND c.topic = gr.topic
             AND c.partition_id = gr.partition_id AND s2.taken_at <= gr.taken_at
           ORDER BY s2.taken_at DESC
           LIMIT 1), 0) AS lag
  FROM grid gr
  JOIN log_end_offsets l
    ON l.snapshot_id = gr.snapshot_id AND l.topic = gr.topic AND l.partition_id = gr.partition_id
), totals AS (
  SELECT group_id, taken_at, SUM(lag) AS total_lag
  FROM lags
  GROUP BY group_id, taken_at
), steps AS (
  SELECT group_id, taken_at, total_lag,
         LAG(total_lag) OVER w AS prev_lag,
         LAG(taken_at)  OVER w AS prev_at
  FROM totals
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY taken_at)
), islands AS (                       -- a new island starts at every step that is not an increase
  SELECT *, COALESCE(total_lag > prev_lag, false) AS up,
         SUM(CASE WHEN total_lag > prev_lag THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY taken_at) AS island
  FROM steps
)
SELECT group_id,
       MIN(prev_at)   AS streak_start,
       MAX(taken_at)  AS streak_end,
       COUNT(*)       AS increases,
       MIN(prev_lag)  AS lag_at_start,
       MAX(total_lag) AS lag_at_end
FROM islands
WHERE up
GROUP BY group_id, island
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{streak}}
ORDER BY group_id, streak_start;

Explanation. First make the lag table dense: every partition a group consumes, at every snapshot from its first commit on. The committed offset at a snapshot is the latest commit at or before it (a carry-forward); below Very Hard every snapshot has a row, so the lookup returns that row. Each partition's lag is clamped at 0 before summing, so a committed offset read a moment after its log-end offset cannot cancel another partition's real lag. Summing gives one total per (group, snapshot). LAG over taken_at (never snapshot_id − 1, because ids have gaps) gives the previous total; a step is an increase only when strictly greater. A running SUM of the non-increase flags numbers the islands, and the increase rows of one island are one streak. Because totals rise strictly within a streak, MIN(prev_lag) is the baseline lag and MAX(total_lag) the final one; MIN(prev_at) is the baseline snapshot.

Complexity. The correlated lookup is an index probe per (group, partition, snapshot) with the primary key; one window sort per group; O(n log n) overall. In production the collector would store the carried-forward offset itself, and streaks would be detected incrementally.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery and Snowflake: LAST_VALUE(committed_offset IGNORE NULLS) OVER (PARTITION BY group_id, topic, partition_id ORDER BY taken_at) over a dense grid replaces the correlated subquery; GREATEST exists in both; COUNTIF/COUNT_IF for flags. Spark SQL: last(committed_offset, true) OVER (…), and window frames for the islands are the same. MySQL 8: window functions and LATERAL exist; GREATEST is fine, but LAG over a CTE is the usual way.

Edge cases built into the data. Snapshot ids with gaps; an equal total between two growth runs (Medium: N − 1 increases, an equal step, then more growth: >= merges them into a false streak); two streaks in one group; Hard: groups consuming two topics, a committed offset above its log-end offset (raw lag negative), a streak of exactly N; Very Hard: rows only when the committed offset changed, a stalled partition with no rows while its lag grows, a partition whose first commit arrives part-way through (its lag joins the total then), and a group whose series starts late.

Common mistakes. Joining on snapshot_id − 1; >= for growth; counting snapshots instead of increases (off by one); reporting the first increased snapshot as the start; clamping the group total instead of each partition (or not clamping); an inner join on snapshot_id that drops partitions without a row, so a stalled partition looks caught up; dense-ranking snapshots per group, which breaks when a group starts late.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Time lag needs the timestamp of the record at the committed offset (or a sample of offset → time from the log); the age of the oldest unconsumed record is the clearer number for people. (2) Keep per-group state (previous total, current run length and baseline) in a stream processor keyed by group; emit when the run reaches N. (3) Annotate known backfills with an expected end and suppress only while lag is draining at the expected rate; a stall (no committed offset change) should still alert. (4) Lag drops to zero with a jump in committed offset larger than the records produced since: detect committed-offset jumps against log-end growth, and alert on offset resets separately.

Rubric anchors. 2: totals per group right but streaks off by one, >=, or id arithmetic. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also handles time lag, incremental detection and offset resets credibly.

Strong signals. Builds the per-group total table first and checks it by hand; asks whether the collector writes a row per snapshot; treats a negative raw lag as a measurement artefact. Red flags. Treating missing rows as zero lag; deriving the previous snapshot from ids.

Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{min_bytes}} and {{k}} are the instance's floor and multiple)

WITH samples AS (                     -- a sample delivered twice counts once
  SELECT DISTINCT topic, partition_id, sample_ts, bytes_in
  FROM bytes_in_samples
), hourly AS (                        -- bytes per partition per hour
  SELECT topic, date_trunc('hour', sample_ts) AS hour_start, partition_id, SUM(bytes_in) AS bytes
  FROM samples
  GROUP BY topic, date_trunc('hour', sample_ts), partition_id
), topic_hours AS (
  SELECT h.topic, h.hour_start, SUM(h.bytes) AS total_bytes,
         (SELECT c.partition_count              -- the count in force at the end of the hour
          FROM partition_count_changes c
          WHERE c.topic = h.topic AND c.effective_at < h.hour_start + INTERVAL '1 hour'
          ORDER BY c.effective_at DESC
          LIMIT 1) AS partitions
  FROM hourly h
  GROUP BY h.topic, h.hour_start
), busiest AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (topic, hour_start) topic, hour_start, partition_id, bytes
  FROM hourly
  ORDER BY topic, hour_start, bytes DESC, partition_id
)
SELECT t.topic, t.hour_start,
       b.partition_id                                         AS busiest_partition,
       b.bytes                                                AS busiest_bytes,
       ROUND(t.total_bytes::numeric / t.partitions, 2)        AS mean_bytes,
       ROUND(b.bytes::numeric * t.partitions / t.total_bytes, 3) AS skew_ratio
FROM topic_hours t
JOIN busiest b USING (topic, hour_start)
WHERE t.total_bytes >= {{min_bytes}}
  AND b.bytes * t.partitions > {{k}} * t.total_bytes        -- no division: exact at the boundary
ORDER BY t.topic, t.hour_start;

Explanation. Aggregate twice: 20-minute samples to per-partition hourly totals, then partitions to topic-hours. DISTINCT first removes samples delivered twice (only present in Very Hard; elsewhere it changes nothing). The partition count is looked up as of the end of the hour (the latest change strictly before the next hour starts), so a partition added at 10:25 counts for the whole 10:00 hour and a change at exactly 11:00 belongs to 11:00. Dividing by the count, not by the number of partitions with rows, keeps idle partitions in the mean. DISTINCT ON with bytes DESC, partition_id picks the busiest partition with the tie-break. The threshold is compared without division (busiest × count > k × total), so a ratio exactly k is never reported because of a rounding artefact; rounding is applied only to the displayed columns.

Complexity. Two hash aggregates and one sort for DISTINCT ON, O(n log n) in the number of samples; the count lookup is one index probe per topic-hour.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(sample_ts, HOUR), QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY topic, hour_start ORDER BY bytes DESC, partition_id) = 1, and an as-of lookup with a correlated subquery or ARRAY_AGG(… ORDER BY effective_at DESC LIMIT 1)[OFFSET(0)]; ROUND on NUMERIC keeps exactness. Snowflake: DATE_TRUNC('hour', …), QUALIFY, and ASOF JOIN for the count. Spark SQL: date_trunc('hour', …), row_number() in a subquery, decimals for exact comparison. MySQL 8: no DISTINCT ON; use ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE.

Edge cases built into the data. Balanced topic-hours; a skewed topic-hour below the floor; Hard: idle partitions with no rows that make an hour skewed only when they count; a ratio of exactly k (not reported); a total exactly at the floor (reported); two partitions tied for busiest; Very Hard: partitions added mid-hour (the count at the hour's end applies) and exactly on an hour boundary, and samples delivered twice.

Common mistakes. Mean over sample rows (AVG(bytes_in)); dividing by the number of partitions that had traffic; comparing the rounded ratio; >= at the boundary; > for the floor; RANK returning two busiest rows on a tie; counting duplicate samples; taking the partition count at the start of the hour or the current count for every hour.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Per-key byte counts from a sample of records (or producer metrics by key hash) separate one heavy key from a hash collision; a producer that sends everything to one partition shows a single partition even with uniform keys. (2) The default hash changes the target partition of existing keys when the count changes, so per-key order across the change is not guaranteed and a compacted topic can hold a key in two partitions; plan a migration or a new topic. (3) Messages per second, consumer lag per partition and leader placement per broker; flag when the hot partition's leader is also the most loaded broker. (4) Pre-aggregate per partition per minute in the stream, keep hourly rollups for a year, and compute the report from rollups.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but mean over traffic-bearing partitions or sample rows, or boundary errors. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains hot-key diagnosis, repartitioning consequences and continuous computation.

Strong signals. Asks where the partition count comes from; avoids division in the threshold; checks the tie-break. Red flags. "Just add partitions" without considering key ordering; treating idle partitions as nonexistent.

Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{window_start}} and {{window_end}} are the instance's day)

WITH bounds AS (
  SELECT TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_start}}' AS ws, TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_end}}' AS we
), spans AS (                          -- each row holds until the partition's next change
  SELECT c.topic, c.partition_id, c.isr_size,
         GREATEST(c.changed_at, b.ws) AS s,
         LEAST(COALESCE(LEAD(c.changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY c.topic, c.partition_id
                                                 ORDER BY c.changed_at), b.we), b.we) AS e
  FROM isr_changes c CROSS JOIN bounds b
), clipped AS (
  SELECT sp.*, t.replication_factor AS rf, t.min_insync_replicas AS min_isr
  FROM spans sp JOIN topics t USING (topic)
  WHERE sp.e > sp.s
), urp AS (
  SELECT topic,
         COUNT(DISTINCT partition_id)          AS under_replicated_partitions,
         SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM e - s))        AS urp_seconds
  FROM clipped
  WHERE isr_size < rf
  GROUP BY topic
), below AS (                          -- below-min intervals of every partition of a topic
  SELECT topic, s, e,
         MAX(e) OVER (PARTITION BY topic ORDER BY s, e
                      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS reach
  FROM clipped
  WHERE isr_size < min_isr
), islands AS (                        -- a new island when an interval starts after everything so far
  SELECT topic, s, e,
         SUM(CASE WHEN reach >= s THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY topic ORDER BY s, e ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS island
  FROM below
), merged AS (
  SELECT topic, SUM(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM island_end - island_start)) AS below_seconds
  FROM (SELECT topic, island, MIN(s) AS island_start, MAX(e) AS island_end
        FROM islands GROUP BY topic, island) m
  GROUP BY topic
)
SELECT u.topic,
       u.under_replicated_partitions,
       ROUND(u.urp_seconds / 60, 2)                     AS urp_partition_minutes,
       ROUND(COALESCE(m.below_seconds, 0) / 60, 2)      AS below_min_isr_minutes
FROM urp u
LEFT JOIN merged m USING (topic)
ORDER BY u.topic;

Explanation. Each change row starts an interval that lasts until the partition's next change. LEAD must run over all rows, before any window filter, so the last change before the window (yesterday's) still produces the interval in force at midnight. Clipping with GREATEST/LEAST and keeping only intervals with end > start drops rows from before and after the window and the change at exactly the window end. Under-replicated time is a plain sum over partitions with isr_size < replication_factor, and COUNT(DISTINCT partition_id) counts partitions, not intervals. Below-min time is per topic, as a union: intervals with isr_size < min_insync_replicas from all partitions are sorted by start, and a new island begins only when an interval starts after the largest end seen so far (MAX(e) over the preceding rows), which handles nested intervals; touching intervals merge, which does not change the total. Topics with no under-replicated time are omitted; a topic with under-replicated time but nothing below the minimum shows 0.

Complexity. One sort per partition for LEAD, one per topic for the island window; O(n log n).

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_DIFF(e, s, SECOND), the same window functions; COUNTIF. Snowflake: DATEDIFF('second', s, e), CONDITIONAL_TRUE_EVENT can number islands. Spark SQL: unix_timestamp(e) - unix_timestamp(s), window frames as here. MySQL 8: TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, s, e); LEAD and running MAX are supported.

Edge cases built into the data. Medium: every partition has a row at the window start; a partition that is under-replicated twice (counted once); at most one partition per topic below the minimum. Hard: state carried in from the previous day, rows after the window and exactly at its end, repeated sizes, overlapping below-min intervals in one topic. Very Hard: per-topic settings including min_insync_replicas equal to the replication factor, a partition whose only row is from the day before, and a nested interval followed by one that starts inside the outer one (a merge against the previous row's end double counts).

Common mistakes. Filtering to the window before LEAD; not clipping at the window end; <= against the minimum; summing below-min time across partitions; merging against the previous row's end; COUNT(*) of intervals as partitions; minute buckets that lose seconds.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Correlate with producer error metrics (NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS responses) per client and topic; the ISR log only says writes would fail. (2) Keep settings as effective-dated rows and split each interval at setting changes before comparing. (3) Alert on a partition's current run length, not on each shrink, with a grace period that covers a rolling restart; page when below-min time starts, not when it ends. (4) Log which replicas left the ISR (or the leader's broker per interval) and attribute minutes to the missing broker; most incidents are one broker.

Rubric anchors. 2: per-partition intervals right but no carry-in, no clipping, or a summed below-min total. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also discusses rejected writes, settings history, alerting and broker attribution.

Strong signals. Asks how the state at midnight is known; draws the overlapping intervals; distinguishes partition-minutes from topic-minutes. Red flags. Expanding the day into minutes and joining (loses seconds, explodes at scale); treating ISR equal to the minimum as unavailable.

def compact(records, active_start, now_ms, delete_retention_ms, min_lag_ms):
    by_part = {p: [] for p in active_start}
    for rec in records:
        by_part[rec[0]].append(rec)
    young = now_ms - min_lag_ms            # a record with ts_ms above this is too young to clean
    horizon = now_ms - delete_retention_ms # a tombstone at or before this is dropped
    out = {}
    for p, recs in by_part.items():
        end = active_start[p]              # first offset that is not cleanable
        for _, off, _, _, ts in recs:
            if off >= end:
                break
            if ts > young:
                end = off
                break
        last = {}                          # key -> its last offset inside the cleanable range
        for _, off, key, _, _ in recs:
            if off >= end:
                break
            last[key] = off
        kept = []
        for _, off, key, value, ts in recs:
            if off >= end:
                kept.append(off)
            elif last[key] == off and not (value is None and ts <= horizon):
                kept.append(off)
        out[p] = kept
    return out

Explanation. Partitions never interact, so the records are grouped by partition (in input order, which is offset order). The cleanable range ends at the active segment, or earlier, at the first record in offset order that is younger than the minimum lag (Very Hard): later records are not cleanable even if their timestamps are older, because the range is a prefix of offsets. One pass over the range stores each key's last offset in it; records outside the range are never added, so a newer record in the active segment does not supersede older ones. A third pass keeps everything outside the range and, inside it, only each key's last record, dropping it when it is a tombstone at or past the horizon. Offsets are preserved, so the result is ascending.

Complexity. O(n) time and O(keys) memory per partition. The timing test (300 000 records over 60 000 keys) runs in about 0.4 s in CPython; a version that rescans the cleaned records once per key did not finish in 60 s.

Dialect notes. Java: a HashMap<String, Long> from key to last offset; C++: unordered_map. In SQL the same answer is ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY partition, key ORDER BY offset DESC) = 1 within the cleanable range, plus the rows outside it. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Several versions of one key; a newer record in the active segment that must not remove older ones; a tombstone exactly at the horizon (dropped) and one millisecond newer (kept); a tombstone followed by a re-insert; Hard: the same key in two partitions, offset gaps, an empty active segment and a partition with no records (empty list); Very Hard: the first too-young record ends the range even though later records are older, and a record exactly at the lag boundary is still cleanable.

Common mistakes. Letting active-segment records supersede older ones; compacting the active segment; one dictionary across partitions; < instead of <= at the horizon; dropping every tombstone or keeping every tombstone; ending the cleanable range at any too-young record found anywhere instead of the first in offset order; returning offsets renumbered from 0; omitting a partition with no records.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Bound the offset map: process the dirty part of the log in chunks that fit the map (several passes), or store key hashes rather than keys and accept rare collisions by verifying against the record. (2) A consumer that starts after the tombstone is dropped sees neither the value nor the delete, so its state keeps the old value: delete_retention_ms should exceed the longest time a consumer can take to read from the beginning. (3) Superseded records remain until their segment is cleaned, so consumers can see several versions of a key; that is allowed, since compaction only promises the last value is kept. (4) A minimum lag gives consumers a window to see every change (not just the latest), at the cost of keeping that much uncompacted data on disk.

Rubric anchors. 2: last-value-per-key right but active segment or horizon rules wrong, or quadratic. 3: all tests pass in O(n). 4: also discusses memory bounds, tombstone retention and what consumers observe.

Strong signals. Asks what the active segment is and why it is excluded; states the boundary comparisons before coding. Red flags. Sorting by timestamp to find the latest record per key (offset order defines "latest" here); treating compaction as deleting old records by age.

def apply_retention(partitions, configs, now_ms):
    out = {}
    for topic, pid, log_start, segs in partitions:
        retention_ms, retention_bytes = configs[topic]
        active = len(segs) - 1                 # index of the active segment: never deleted
        i = 0                                  # segments[:i] are deleted
        if retention_ms != -1:                 # 1. time: stop at the first one not expired
            while i < active and now_ms - segs[i][2] > retention_ms:
                i += 1
        if retention_bytes != -1:              # 2. size: one running total of what is left
            remaining = sum(size for _, size, _ in segs[i:])
            while i < active and remaining - segs[i][1] >= retention_bytes:
                remaining -= segs[i][1]
                i += 1
        while i < active and segs[i + 1][0] <= log_start:   # 3. below the log start offset
            i += 1
        deleted_bytes = sum(size for _, size, _ in segs[:i])
        out[(topic, pid)] = (i, deleted_bytes, max(log_start, segs[i][0]))
    return out

Explanation. Every rule deletes from the oldest end, so the state is one index i: segments before it are deleted. Time deletion advances while the oldest remaining segment has expired (strictly older than retention_ms) and stops at the first that has not, even if later ones have. The size step computes the remaining total once, including the active segment, and advances while removing the next segment would leave at least retention_bytes, subtracting as it goes. def apply_retention(partitions, configs, now_ms):
    out = {}
    for topic, pid, log_start, segs in partitions:
        retention_ms, retention_bytes = configs[topic]
        active = len(segs) - 1                 # index of the active segment: never deleted
        i = 0                                  # segments[:i] are deleted
        if retention_ms != -1:                 # 1. time: stop at the first one not expired
            while i < active and now_ms - segs[i][2] > retention_ms:
                i += 1
        if retention_bytes != -1:              # 2. size: one running total of what is left
            remaining = sum(size for _, size, _ in segs[i:])
            while i < active and remaining - segs[i][1] >= retention_bytes:
                remaining -= segs[i][1]
                i += 1
        while i < active and segs[i + 1][0] <= log_start:   # 3. below the log start offset
            i += 1
        deleted_bytes = sum(size for _, size, _ in segs[:i])
        out[(topic, pid)] = (i, deleted_bytes, max(log_start, segs[i][0]))
    return out

import heapq


def rebalance(partitions, members, owned):
    if not members:
        return {}
    exists = set(partitions)
    group = set(members)
    claim = {}                                   # partition -> (generation, member or None)
    for member, generation, parts in owned:
        if member not in group:
            continue                             # a member that left keeps nothing
        for p in parts:
            if p not in exists:
                continue                         # the partition was deleted
            cur = claim.get(p)
            if cur is None or generation > cur[0]:
                claim[p] = (generation, member)
            elif generation == cur[0] and cur[1] != member:
                claim[p] = (generation, None)    # a tie at the top generation: nobody keeps it
    retained = {m: [] for m in members}
    for p, (_g, m) in claim.items():
        if m is not None:
            retained[m].append(p)

    q, extra = divmod(len(partitions), len(members))
    by_load = sorted(members, key=lambda m: (-len(retained[m]), m))
    quota = {m: q + (1 if i < extra else 0) for i, m in enumerate(by_load)}

    result, kept = {}, set()
    for m in members:
        keep = sorted(retained[m])[:quota[m]]    # keep the lowest, release the highest
        result[m] = keep
        kept.update(keep)

    heap = [(len(result[m]), m) for m in members if len(result[m]) < quota[m]]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    for p in sorted(p for p in partitions if p not in kept):
        load, m = heapq.heappop(heap)
        result[m].append(p)
        if load + 1 < quota[m]:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (load + 1, m))
    for m in members:
        result[m].sort()
    return result

Explanation. The answer is fixed by the four rules, so the work is to apply them in the right order and fast. Claims are resolved in one pass: each partition keeps the best (generation, member) seen so far, and a second claim at the same top generation from a different member marks it unowned. A claim from a member that left, or on a partition that no longer exists, is skipped. Quotas come from one sort of the members by (-retained, id). Giving the P mod C extra places to the members that retain the most maximises Σ min(retainedᵢ, quotaᵢ), which is exactly the number of partitions that stay put, so no balanced assignment moves fewer. Each member keeps the lowest of its retained partitions up to its quota. The free partitions, sorted, are placed with a heap keyed by (load, member) that holds only members below quota. Popping gives the least-loaded member with room and the smaller id on ties, and the member goes back in only if it still has room. The heap never runs dry, because the quotas add up to P.

Complexity. O(P log P) for sorting partitions, O(C log C) for the quotas, and O(F log C) for placing F free partitions. The timing test (200 000 partitions, 3 900 members, about 150 000 free) runs in about 0.8 s in CPython. Scanning every member for each free partition is O(F·C), about 6·10⁸ steps, and did not finish in 60 s.

Dialect notes. In Java the same structure is a PriorityQueue of members with a comparator on (load, id), and partitions are compared on (topic, partition) with Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparingInt(...). Kafka's own assignors live in the client library; real sticky assignors also aim at balance first and stickiness second, but their tie-breaking differs from this exercise's rules. A SQL formulation (row numbers per member for keeps, then a window over free partitions) is possible for the quota step but awkward for the heap step. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A fresh group with no claims; one member leaving; one member joining, so members above quota release their highest partitions; more members than partitions; equal retained counts, where the extra place goes to the smaller id; claims from a member that left; a partition count that divides evenly; an empty group ({}); partition numbers 2 and 10, which must sort numerically; (Hard) a new partition and a claim on a deleted partition, and joins and leaves together; (Very Hard) a duplicate claim won by the newer generation, and one at the same generation that leaves the partition unowned.

Common mistakes. Assigning from scratch with round robin or ranges (balanced, but it moves most partitions); keeping every retained partition and only balancing the rest (an overloaded member stays overloaded); giving the extra places by member id instead of by retained count (balanced, but moves more and fails the tests); releasing the lowest partitions instead of the highest; sorting partitions as strings such as "orders-10"; letting a same-generation tie go to the first claimant in input order; counting a departed member's claims; scanning members per partition.

Follow-up guidance. (1) In the classic consumer group protocol the coordinator picks one member as the group leader, the leader runs the assignor with every member's subscription and owned partitions, and the coordinator distributes the result. Newer protocol versions move assignment to the broker; check current docs. Each member must send its subscription and what it owned, with its generation. (2) That is the cooperative (incremental) idea: compare old and new ownership, revoke only partitions that change owner, and assign them in a second round, so the rest keep consuming. (3) Weighted quotas: share P in proportion to capacity with a largest-remainder rule. "Fewest moves" is still Σ min(retained, quota), maximised the same way. (4) Balancing by load is a bin-packing problem. Good answers bound the movement per rebalance (move only while imbalance is above a threshold), use measured rates with smoothing, and accept a little imbalance to avoid churn.

Rubric anchors. 2: a balanced assignment that ignores stickiness, or a sticky one that is not balanced; several edge tests fail. 3: all tests pass, with a heap or an equivalent O(log C) placement. 4: also proves why the quota rule minimises moves, resolves claims in one pass, and gives a convincing account of cooperative rebalancing and weighted load.

Strong signals. Computes quotas before placing anything; asks how ties at the top generation are resolved; notices that sorting partition names as strings is wrong. Red flags. "Just reassign everything round robin, it's balanced"; no estimate of the cost of scanning members per partition.

def visible_records(log, high_watermark, start=0, isolation="read_committed"):
    if isolation == "read_uncommitted":
        return [o for o, _p, kind in log
                if start <= o < high_watermark and kind in ("data", "txn")]
    open_txn = {}                  # producer -> offsets of its open transaction, in order
    committed = set()
    for o, p, kind in log:
        if o >= high_watermark:
            break                  # not replicated yet: neither records nor markers count
        if kind == "txn":
            open_txn.setdefault(p, []).append(o)
        elif kind == "commit" or kind == "abort":
            offsets = open_txn.pop(p, None)      # a marker with no open transaction does nothing
            if offsets and kind == "commit":
                committed.update(offsets)
    lso = min((offs[0] for offs in open_txn.values()), default=high_watermark)
    out = []
    for o, _p, kind in log:
        if o >= lso:
            break
        if o >= start and (kind == "data" or (kind == "txn" and o in committed)):
            out.append(o)
    return out

Explanation. One forward sweep up to the high watermark keeps, for each producer, the offsets of its open transaction. A "txn" record joins its producer's open transaction (creating one if needed). A marker pops that producer's open transaction: on commit its offsets become committed, on abort they are dropped, and a marker with nothing open does nothing. Entries at or above the high watermark are not visible, so the sweep stops there, and a marker beyond it leaves its transaction open. Whatever is still open sets the last stable offset: the smallest first offset among open transactions, which can be below start. A second pass returns offsets in [start, lso) that are non-transactional or committed. read_uncommitted needs no transaction state at all.

Complexity. O(n) time, O(n) memory in the worst case for open transactions and committed offsets. The timing test (300 000 entries, 200 producers, about 7 000 aborted transactions) runs in about 0.2 s in CPython. Checking each record against the list of aborted transactions did not finish in 40 s, and scanning ahead from each record to its producer's next marker took about 20 s.

Dialect notes. In Kafka's Java consumer the broker returns, with each fetch, the aborted transactions (producer id and first offset) that overlap the fetched range, and the client filters batch by batch: it adds a producer to an "aborted" set when it reaches that first offset and removes it at the producer's abort marker. That keeps memory bounded per fetch instead of per log. A SQL version is a window per producer that numbers transactions by counting earlier markers, then a join to each transaction's ending marker. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Committed and aborted transactions interleaved with non-transactional records; an open transaction that stops the read at its first record, including non-transactional records after it; a committed transaction with records above the last stable offset; two transactions in a row from one producer; only non-transactional records; an empty log; (Hard) a commit marker exactly at the high watermark, a start offset part-way in, and read_uncommitted returning aborted records; (Very Hard) markers with no open transaction, an open transaction that began before start (nothing returned), and gaps in offsets.

Common mistakes. Returning non-transactional records past the last stable offset; reading markers at or above the high watermark; treating a stray marker as ending the producer's next transaction; returning a committed transaction's records above the last stable offset; computing the last stable offset only from records at or after start; returning marker offsets; for read_uncommitted, dropping aborted records; per-record scans of all aborted transactions.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The last stable offset is stuck at the hung transaction's first record, so every read_committed consumer of that partition stops advancing, and their lag grows while producers keep writing. It clears when the transaction times out and is aborted. Watch the gap between high watermark and last stable offset, and open transaction age. (2) Use the aborted-transaction list with first offsets: walk batches in order, track aborted producers in a set, and drop their records until their abort marker. (3) Consume-transform-produce in one transaction, with offsets committed in the same transaction, gives exactly-once between topics. A database sink needs idempotent writes or offsets stored in the database's own transaction. (4) Compaction can remove aborted records and, after the transaction is fully cleaned, the markers too, but only after a retention period, so that consumers in the middle of a read still see a marker. Strong candidates say the exact rules are version-dependent and point to the docs.

Rubric anchors. 2: filters aborted records but ignores the last stable offset or the high watermark; several edge tests fail. 3: all tests pass with a linear sweep. 4: also explains why the last stable offset exists (a transaction could still commit, and ordering must hold), answers the hung-transaction and batch-by-batch questions with specifics.

Strong signals. Asks what happens to a marker beyond the high watermark; notices that non-transactional records are cut off by the last stable offset too. Red flags. "Just skip aborted records" with no notion of open transactions; sorting the log.

# (writer type -> reader types that can read it)
PROMOTIONS = {
    "int": {"long", "float", "double"},
    "long": {"float", "double"},
    "float": {"double"},
    "string": {"bytes"},
    "bytes": {"string"},
}


def _type_ok(reader_type, writer_type):
    if isinstance(reader_type, dict) and isinstance(writer_type, dict):
        # enums: every symbol the writer can produce must exist in the reader,
        # unless the reader has a default symbol to fall back on
        return set(writer_type["enum"]) <= set(reader_type["enum"]) or "default" in reader_type
    if isinstance(reader_type, dict) or isinstance(writer_type, dict):
        return False                     # an enum and a primitive never match
    return reader_type == writer_type or reader_type in PROMOTIONS.get(writer_type, ())


def _unreadable_fields(reader, writer):
    """Names of the reader's fields it cannot fill from data written with writer."""
    written = {f["name"]: f for f in writer["fields"]}
    bad = []
    for rf in reader["fields"]:
        wf = written.get(rf["name"])
        if wf is None:
            if "default" not in rf:      # a default of 0, "", False or None is still a default
                bad.append(rf["name"])
        elif not _type_ok(rf["type"], wf["type"]):
            bad.append(rf["name"])
        elif wf.get("optional") and not rf.get("optional"):
            bad.append(rf["name"])       # the writer may send null; the reader cannot hold it
    return bad


def check_compatibility(new_schema, previous, mode):
    """previous: registered versions, oldest first (version 1 is previous[0]).
    Return sorted [version, "backward" | "forward", field] conflicts; [] if compatible."""
    if mode == "NONE" or not previous:
        return []
    versions = list(range(1, len(previous) + 1))
    if not mode.endswith("_TRANSITIVE"):
        versions = versions[-1:]         # only the latest version
    base = mode.replace("_TRANSITIVE", "")
    conflicts = []
    for v in versions:
        old = previous[v - 1]
        if base in ("BACKWARD", "FULL"):          # the new schema reads old data
            conflicts += [[v, "backward", f] for f in _unreadable_fields(new_schema, old)]
        if base in ("FORWARD", "FULL"):           # old schemas read new data
            conflicts += [[v, "forward", f] for f in _unreadable_fields(old, new_schema)]
    return sorted(conflicts)

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Promotion checked in the wrong direction. PROMOTIONS maps a writer type to the reader types that can read it, but _type_ok looks up the reader's type and tests the writer's. Symptom: widening int to long is rejected under BACKWARD, and narrowing long to int is accepted and breaks consumers. Fix: reader_type in PROMOTIONS.get(writer_type, ()).
  2. Falsy default treated as no default. if not rf.get("default") treats 0, "", False and None as missing. Symptom: a new field with default 0, or an optional field with a null default, is rejected. Fix: if "default" not in rf.
  3. Reader enum default ignored. The enum check requires every writer symbol to be a reader symbol even when the reader's enum has a default symbol. Symptom: adding a symbol is rejected under FORWARD although the old enum has a default. Fix: ... or "default" in reader_type.
  4. The oldest version checked instead of the latest. previous is oldest first, and versions[:1] takes version 1. Symptom: a schema compatible with the latest version is rejected because of an old one, and a breaking change against the latest can pass. Fix: versions[-1:].
  5. Optional rule reversed. The code flags a reader that is optional when the writer is required, which is safe, and misses a writer that may send null to a reader that cannot hold it. Symptom: making an optional field required passes BACKWARD, and old records with nulls fail to read. Fix: elif wf.get("optional") and not rf.get("optional").

Each bug has its own failing checks and passes the others: widening and narrowing (1), default 0 and null default (2), the enum with a default symbol (3), the two-version non-transitive case (4), and optional to required and back (5). The "new field without a default" and "enum without an old default" checks pass on the original code, which is worth noting: the buggy checker is not wrong everywhere.

Explanation. Every mode reduces to one question asked in one or both directions: can this reader schema read data written with that writer schema? Getting the reader and the writer right is the whole problem. BACKWARD makes the new schema the reader of old data. FORWARD makes the old schema the reader of new data. Promotions, optional fields and enum symbols all depend on which side is which. Defaults matter only on the reader's side, for fields the writer does not have, and their presence is what counts.

Complexity. O(V·F) for V versions checked and F fields, with a dict per writer schema. The timing test (300 versions of 300 fields, FULL_TRANSITIVE) runs in about 0.15 s in CPython.

Dialect notes. The registry's real checks use the Avro library's schema resolution, which also covers nested records, unions, arrays, maps, aliases, logical types and fixed sizes. Protobuf and JSON Schema have different rules: in Protobuf, renaming a field is wire-compatible but changing a field number is not. In Java, SchemaCompatibility.checkReaderWriterCompatibility(reader, writer) from the Avro library takes the reader first, which is the same trap as bug 1 at API level. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Widening and narrowing; a new field with default 0; a new optional field with a null default; new fields without a default, optional or not; removing a field the old schema needs under FORWARD; enum symbols added with and without an old default symbol; a two-version history under a non-transitive mode; optional to required and required to optional; NONE; an enum against a string; nothing registered; (Hard) FULL in both directions; (Very Hard) a transitive mode over every version and FULL_TRANSITIVE with enum defaults.

Common mistakes. Fixing the promotion bug by swapping the arguments at the call sites, which also swaps the default and optional logic; replacing not rf.get("default") with rf.get("default") is None, which still rejects a null default; making transitive mode check only the latest; letting optional imply a default; rewriting the checker instead of making minimal fixes.

(1) Under FULL_TRANSITIVE a rename is add-new-field-with-default, migrate producers and consumers to write and read both, then remove the old field once every registered version and every consumer allows it. It takes several releases, and some teams use a new subject instead. (2) A consumer on an old schema reading new data is a forward problem: BACKWARD does not protect it. If consumers upgrade after producers, the subject needs FORWARD or FULL. (3) Semantic changes (a field's unit changes from cents to dollars), producers that bypass the registry, consumers using a different reader schema than assumed, or a mode changed on the subject after the fact. (4) Check the shared type against every subject that references it, under each subject's own mode, and block the change if any fails.

CFL-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Collection. A collector per cluster, sharded by group id across a few workers. Every {{sample_every}} it lists groups, reads committed offsets per group with batched admin calls, and reads log-end offsets once per partition, shared by every group that reads it, not once per group. Each sample is (cluster, group, topic, partition, committed_offset, log_end_offset, sampled_at), with the group's state (stable, rebalancing, empty) and generation.
  • Time lag. Two estimates, both kept. (a) Rate-based: offset lag divided by the partition's recent produce rate, from log-end deltas. It is cheap, but wrong on bursty or quiet topics. (b) Timestamp-based: for partitions with lag, look up the timestamp of the record at the committed offset (a single-record fetch or an offset-for-timestamp index, cached per partition and offset), so time lag = now − that timestamp. It is exact when timestamps are sane. Use (b) for paging where available, clamp negative values, and flag timestamps outside a sane window.
  • State per partition. Over a sliding window of N samples: is the committed offset moving? Is lag shrinking, flat or growing? Classify as OK, catching up, stalled (committed offset still while log-end moves), stopped (no commit for longer than the group's commit interval allows, even with small lag), or idle (log-end not moving, lag zero or tiny). Roll up per group as the worst partition, plus the count of affected partitions.
  • Alerting. Per group: raise when the time lag exceeds {{page_after}} for M consecutive samples, or the group is stalled for longer than its tolerance; clear only when lag is below a lower threshold for K samples (hysteresis). Suppress while the group is rebalancing, but escalate if rebalancing lasts longer than a bound. Thresholds live in a config store per group, owned by the team, with platform defaults. Alerts carry partitions, onset time and a link to the lag chart.
  • Storage and cost. Keep raw per-partition samples for a short window (hours) in a store sized for it, and keep per-group rollups (max time lag, total offset lag, stalled partition count) as long-lived metrics. That avoids millions of long-lived series at {{partitions}} partitions. Deleted groups are detected by the listing and their alerts closed.

Competing designs to accept. Exporting per-partition lag as metrics to a time-series system with recording rules for group rollups (accept if cardinality is addressed); a streaming job that reads the internal offsets topic and log-end offsets and computes lag continuously; client-side lag metrics from consumers that publish them (accept as a complement, since not every consumer can be changed). Open-source lag checkers that evaluate a sliding window of offsets are a reasonable reference point.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Fetching log-end offsets per group rather than per partition; one admin call per partition; timestamp lookups for every partition every cycle; series cardinality; alerts on instantaneous values; rebalances paging; stale alerts for deleted groups; producer clock skew; the collector itself lagging and producing gaps that look like stalls.

Incident guidance.

  • A third of the groups rebalance every few minutes for an hour: alerts are suppressed while each group is rebalancing, but a group that spends most of a window rebalancing is a problem in itself, so raise one aggregated alert ("rebalance storm after client upgrade") rather than thousands of pages. Correlate with the deploy, and show time spent rebalancing per group.
  • Records stamped nine hours in the future: timestamp-based time lag goes negative or tiny. Clamp, flag the topic's timestamps as untrusted, and fall back to the rate-based estimate for it. Tell the producer team, and record the skew as a data quality signal.
  • The collector falls behind: samples arrive late and uneven, and a naive rule would read the gaps as stalls. Store sampled_at and compute rates from actual intervals. Mark windows with missing samples as unknown, never as stalled. Shard the collector further or reduce timestamp lookups to lagging partitions only, and alert on the collector's own cycle time.

Follow-up guidance. (1) With suppression during rebalancing and a bound on how long that can last, nothing pages for short rebalances, and a 20-minute storm raises one rebalancing alert, not a lag page. After the jump, lag recovers and no alert fires. (2) Time lag goes negative; clamp and flag it, and use the rate-based estimate. (3) No: lag is zero and log-end is not moving, so it is idle, not lagging. It becomes a problem only if new records arrive and the committed offset does not move, which the stalled rule catches. (4) Sample quiet or healthy groups less often, keep lagging ones at full rate, and compute timestamps only for partitions with lag. You lose resolution on how fast healthy groups recover. (5) Use the recent net consume rate (consume minus produce). Show it only when the rate has been stable over the window and the forecast horizon is short; never extrapolate across a rebalance or a burst.

Rubric anchors. 2: one offset-lag threshold for every group, evaluated on instantaneous values; no time lag; no stall detection. 3: offset and time lag defined, window-based states including stalled and idle, hysteresis, per-group thresholds, collection costed. 4: also timestamp failure modes handled, rebalances and collector gaps treated explicitly, cardinality controlled with rollups, and each incident answered concretely.

Strong signals. Separates "is the committed offset moving" from "how far behind is it"; asks whose clock sets the timestamp; reads log-end offsets once per partition. Red flags. "Page when lag > 10 000"; a design that cannot tell an idle topic from a stuck consumer.

CFL-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Classify errors. Conversion (deserialising or schema lookup failures), transformation (a single-message transform fails), and write errors. Write errors split into transient (timeouts, throttling, target unavailable: retried with backoff up to a bound, never dead-lettered) and deterministic per-record rejects (a value too large, a constraint violation: dead-lettered). Unknown errors are retried a few times, then treated as deterministic.
  • Dead-letter topic. One per connector (or per source topic for shared connectors), named after it, with the same access control as the source topic and the same or shorter retention. Keyed like the source, so per-key order survives. Each record keeps the original key, value and headers, with context headers added: source topic, partition and offset, connector and task, failure stage, error class and message (truncated, scrubbed of values), first-failure time, and attempt count. Configure the framework to add context headers where it can, and add the rest in the connector's error path.
  • Tolerance with a guard. Tolerate individual bad records, but stop the connector when the dead-letter rate exceeds a threshold over a window (for example 5% over 5 minutes) or a count per hour, because a flood means a deploy problem, not bad records. Stopping keeps the source offsets in place, so nothing is lost.
  • Restarts. The connector commits source offsets only after a record is written or dead-lettered, so a restart reprocesses from the last commit. Dead-letter writes can repeat after a crash, so deduplicate by (source topic, partition, offset) at replay time, not at write time.
  • Monitoring. Dead-letter records per minute per connector and per error class, age of the oldest unreplayed record, and the ratio to records processed. Alerts go to the owning team of the source topic, with a link to sample records (masked) and the error class.
  • Replay. A replay tool reads the dead-letter topic for one connector and an error class or offset range, applies the fix (a new converter, a schema mapping, or corrected data from the producer), and writes to the target through the same idempotent path: upsert by key with a version check (source offset or record timestamp) so an older replayed value never overwrites a newer one. For append-only targets, deduplicate on (source topic, partition, offset) stored as a column. The tool records which dead-letter offsets it has replayed, and completeness is proven by reconciling the set of dead-lettered source offsets against those written to the target.
  • Personal data. Dead-letter topics inherit the source's classification and retention, and erasure jobs cover them. Error messages must not copy field values into headers.

Competing designs to accept. Dead-lettering to object storage instead of a topic (accept if ordering, access and replay are addressed); a quarantine table in the target itself with a status column; a central dead-letter service shared by all connectors with per-team partitioning and access control. Each is fine if records keep their source coordinates and replay is idempotent.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Dead-lettering transient errors (a target outage empties the topic into the dead-letter topic); tolerance without a rate guard; dead-letter topics with broader access than the source; context headers that copy personal data; replays that overwrite newer values; replays run twice; dead-letter retention shorter than the time teams need to fix things; no owner, so dead-lettered records sit forever.

Incident guidance.

  • 40% of one topic's records are dead-lettered after a producer deploy: the rate guard stops that connector within minutes, its source offsets stay put, and the alert names the error class and the producing team. The producer rolls back or fixes, and the connector restarts from its committed offsets. Records already dead-lettered are replayed with the fix, deduplicated by source offset.
  • The target refuses writes for 25 minutes: these are transient errors, so they are retried with backoff and nothing is dead-lettered. When the retry bound is reached, the connector fails and is restarted by the platform once the target is back, from its committed offsets. Lag grows and recovers. A design that dead-letters here creates millions of replays.
  • A replay started twice: the replay tool takes a lock per connector and error class, and both runs write through the idempotent path, so the target is unchanged by the second run. Append-only targets rely on the (topic, partition, offset) deduplication column. The replay ledger shows the double run.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The rate guard stops the connector; good records behind the flood wait instead of being mixed with 40% losses; one alert to the producer team; resume after the fix. (2) Read the dead-letter topic by connector and error class, apply the fix, write through the idempotent upsert path with version checks, throttle to protect the live connector, track replayed offsets, and reconcile at the end. (3) Compare versions: the source offset (or a record version or timestamp) is stored with each row, and the write is conditional on it being newer. (4) Easy if dead-letter topics are keyed and classified like the source and replay copies are tracked; hard if records were copied into tickets, logs or headers. (5) A daily report per team from the dead-letter topic and the replay ledger: unreplayed records by error class and age, with links.

Rubric anchors. 2: "set tolerance to all and send errors to a dead-letter topic", with no context, no guard and no replay plan. 3: errors classified with transient retries, dead-letter topics with full source context and access control, a rate guard, idempotent replay. 4: also per-key ordering on replay, completeness proven by source offsets, personal data handled in dead-letter copies, and each incident answered concretely.

Strong signals. Refuses to dead-letter transient errors; keeps source topic, partition and offset as the record's identity; asks how the target resolves an older value arriving late. Red flags. Skipping errors silently; replay by "just reset the connector's offsets" with no thought for duplicates.

CFL-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Registry mirror (append-only, fed by the registry).
    • subjects (subject_name, naming_strategy topic|record|topic_record, first_seen_at, deleted_at NULL, deletion_kind soft|hard NULL).
    • subject_versions (subject_name, version, schema_id, schema_type avro|protobuf|json, registered_at, registered_by, change_request_id NULL); schemas (schema_id, fingerprint, schema_text). Ids and version numbers are copied from the registry, never assigned here; the same schema_id under two subjects is two version rows pointing at one schema.
    • compatibility_settings (subject_name NULL = global, mode, valid_from, valid_to, set_by, exception_id NULL): a new row per change, so "which mode was in force when version 7 was registered" is an interval lookup.
    • topic_subjects (topic, subject_name, role key|value|event_type, valid_from, valid_to): explicit, because record-name strategies break the one-to-one mapping.
  • Governance (owned here).
    • teams, subject_owners (subject_name, team_id, valid_from, valid_to, assigned_by); a subject without a current owner is a finding.
    • schema_fields (subject_name, version, field_path, type, has_default, is_optional), extracted when a version is registered.
    • field_tags (subject_name, field_path, tag e.g. pii.email|pii.name|confidential, valid_from_version, valid_to_version NULL, tagged_by, reviewed_at). On a new version, tags carry forward for paths that still exist; a renamed path is matched by an explicit rename declaration in the change request (or a field alias in the schema) and carries its tag; a new path is unclassified until reviewed, and a policy blocks publishing an unclassified field to topics readable outside the owner.
    • dependencies (subject_name, team_id, role producer|consumer, source declared|observed, client_id or consumer_group, first_seen_at, last_seen_at): observed from consumer groups reading the topic and from clients fetching schema ids, declared through the change process; observed wins for "who reads", declared for "who must sign".
    • change_requests (request_id, subject_name, proposed_schema_fingerprint, kind compatible|breaking, check_result per mode, migration_plan, status, created_by, created_at), approvals (request_id, approver, decision, decided_at), acknowledgements (request_id, team_id, acked_at), exceptions (exception_id, subject_name, mode, reason, approved_by, valid_from, expires_at).
  • Change flow. CI on the producer's repository runs the registry's compatibility check against the subject's mode (and, for transitive modes, all versions) and the classification check (no unclassified fields) before merge; registration happens from the pipeline with a service identity, not from laptops; a breaking change goes to a new subject or topic (orders.v2) with a dual-write or migration plan unless an approved request with all acknowledgements exists; mode changes to none only through an exception that expires.
  • Sync. The registry's own storage is an internal Kafka topic in the self-managed product; most teams read changes through the registry's REST API on a schedule or through audit logs where available. A reconciliation job compares the registry's subjects and versions with the mirror daily; anything registered outside the process becomes an unowned or unapproved finding, not a silent insert.
  • Queries. Personal-data subjects read by other teams: field_tags (current) ⋈ topic_subjects ⋈ dependencies (observed consumers) where team ≠ current owner. Compatibility history: compatibility_settings ordered by valid_from with exception_id. Version current at time t: subject_versions with max registered_at ≤ t per subject (mapped from the topic through topic_subjects at t).

Competing designs to accept. Using the registry's own tags or metadata features (the public docs describe tags and data-contract metadata; check current docs) as the store for classification, with this model reading them, provided history and approvals are still append-only somewhere. A single event log of governance events with projections. Schema-level rather than field-level tags only at Medium, if the candidate states what is lost.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Treating subject = topic; tags at subject level only (cannot say which field); tags lost on rename; compatibility history not captured (the "02:00 none" problem); consumers known only by declaration (stale); approvals in chat instead of records; reconciliation absent so out-of-process registrations go unnoticed; hard deletes of versions still referenced by retained messages.

Incident guidance.

  • Compatibility set to none for a hotfix: contain by restoring the mode and registering a compatible version (re-adding the field with a default) so consumers can read new messages; identify messages produced with the incompatible schema by schema id and decide whether consumers skip, dead-letter or reprocess them. Guardrail: mode changes only through expiring exceptions, configuration changes mirrored with actor, and an alert on any change to none.
  • Tag did not follow a rename: tag the new path, find every topic and sink that received it since the version was registered, and run the data-handling procedure for the copies. Guardrail: new fields are unclassified by default and block publication to broadly readable topics; renames must be declared in the change request.
  • Near-copy subjects to dodge review: the review queue for {{breaking_requests}} requests a month is the root cause. Add a fast path (compatible changes auto-approve in CI), give breaking changes an SLA, and make subject creation require an owner; sweep unowned subjects to their producing team by observed producer.

Follow-up guidance. (1) One subject_versions row (version 7, schema id), schema_fields rows for the new version, tags carried forward, the new optional field unclassified unless declared, and the change request with its check result. (2) A declared rename or alias carries the tag; otherwise the field is new, untagged and blocked from broad topics. (3) The mirror shows the mode change, its actor, no exception and the version registered under it; an expiring-exception requirement and an alert on mode changes would have prevented it. (4) Observed consumers from consumer groups and schema-id fetches, freshness = last_seen_at; unknown consumers are listed and the owner signs for them. (5) Event feed or polling plus a daily reconciliation; out-of-process subjects become findings with an owner assigned by observed producer.

Rubric anchors. 2: an owners table and a list of subjects, no history, tags at subject level. 3: registry mirror with versions and compatibility history, explicit topic-subject mapping, field-path tags carried across versions, dependencies and a change flow with approval. 4: also renames, exceptions with expiry, observed versus declared consumers, reconciliation against the registry and deletions recorded with their effect on retained data.

Strong signals. Separates what the registry owns from what governance owns; knows which side upgrades first under backward and forward. Red flags. Re-numbering schema ids; letting anyone set compatibility to none; classification that requires reading payloads.

CFL-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Topics.
    • orders.events (delete policy, 30 days): typed events keyed by order_id, {{partitions}} partitions. Events: OrderCreated, ItemsChanged, PaymentAuthorised, OrderPacked, ShipmentDispatched (one per shipment), OrderDelivered, OrderCancelled, RefundIssued.
    • orders.state (compacted): key order_id, value the full current order (not a diff), written by a stream processor from orders.events or by the service itself in the same publish path. New services bootstrap here, then follow orders.events (or follow orders.state alone if they only need state).
  • Envelope. Key: order_id only (stable, so hashing is stable). Headers: event_id (UUID), event_type, schema_id if not in the payload's wire format, producer, correlation_id, causation_id, trace context. Value: order_id, seq (per-order version, 1, 2, 3…), occurred_at, merchant_id, customer_id, the event body. The wire format carries the schema id prefix when a schema registry serializer is used.
  • Publishing. Transactional outbox: the order row change and an outbox row (event_id, order_id, seq, payload) commit in one database transaction; a relay (polling or CDC on the outbox table) publishes in seq order per order with an idempotent producer; a crash after publish and before marking sent republishes, which consumers absorb by event_id or seq. CDC directly on the order tables is acceptable if the event semantics are reconstructed downstream.
  • Ordering guarantees. Per order only (one key, one partition). The producer runs with idempotence enabled, which keeps order with up to five in-flight requests (check current docs), or with one in-flight request. Consumers keep the last applied seq per order: seq ≤ last is a duplicate or stale update and is dropped; seq > last + 1 is a gap, parked and retried or fetched from the state topic.
  • Per-customer ordering. Not provided by the order topic. The notifications team re-keys by customer_id in its own processor (a repartition topic) and orders by occurred_at within a customer; cost: an extra topic and cross-partition timing, so ordering is by event time with a small buffer, not a guarantee.
  • Partition growth. Do not add partitions in place for a keyed topic whose consumers need per-key ordering. Create a new topic with the target count, dual-write or switch producers at a quiesce point per key, let consumers drain the old topic before reading the new one (or switch per order when its last event in the old topic is consumed). Size {{partitions}} up front with headroom.
  • Erasure. Write a tombstone for the order key in orders.state; the old value is removed only after compaction has run past it and the tombstone itself is removed after delete.retention.ms (this exercise's rule; check current docs); a consumer that reads slower than that can miss the tombstone. The event topic ages out at 30 days, or personal data is kept out of events (reference ids only, or field-level encryption with per-customer keys that are destroyed: crypto-shredding). Consumers' copies need their own deletion path driven by an erasure event.

Competing designs to accept. Event sourcing with Kafka as the log of record (the service's state rebuilt from the event topic), if they handle the read-your-writes problem. State topic only, with consumers diffing states, for small consumer counts. Per-event-type topics, if they explain how per-order ordering across types is kept (usually it is lost, so a single topic per aggregate is preferred).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Keying by merchant (hot partition), by customer (fine for ordering but uneven), or no key (ordering lost); diffs instead of full state in the compacted topic (bootstrap needs all history); dual writes without an outbox; adding partitions in place; tombstones that consumers miss; personal data in a 30-day event log; consumers that trust delivery order without seq.

Incident guidance.

  • Outbox relay republished a batch: duplicates are expected under at-least-once relay. Contain by deduplicating notifications on event_id (a recent-ids store) or on (order_id, seq); fix the relay to mark rows sent in small batches. Guardrail: consumer idempotency is part of the contract, tested with replayed batches.
  • State topic re-keyed by merchant: the hot partition is the merchant's {{hot_merchant_share}}. Roll back to order-id keys; serve merchant dashboards from an aggregate keyed by merchant and time bucket (pre-aggregated, so the hot merchant's volume is reduced) or from the warehouse. Guardrail: key changes on shared topics go through review with a partition-skew check.
  • Partitions doubled in place: per-order ordering broke for in-flight orders. Contain: consumers use seq to park out-of-order events and request state; reconcile affected orders from orders.state. Guardrail: partition increases on keyed topics require a migration plan; restrict the permission.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Key order_id; headers event_id/type/trace; value with seq and occurred_at. (2) A customer-keyed derived topic, at the cost of a repartition and event-time ordering only. (3) New topic and switch-over, never in-place growth for ordered consumers. (4) Tombstone, compaction, delete.retention.ms, crypto-shredding or reference-only events, and downstream deletion. (5) Idempotence on (or one in-flight request); seq protects regardless.

Rubric anchors. 2: one topic keyed by merchant or unkeyed, no seq, dual writes. 3: order-id keys, event and compacted state topics, envelope with event_id and seq, outbox or CDC, per-order ordering only. 4: also safe partition growth, per-customer ordering as a derived stream, erasure with tombstones and copies, and the producer settings that preserve order.

Strong signals. States the ordering guarantee before choosing the key; keeps full state, not diffs, in the compacted topic. Red flags. "Kafka guarantees order" without "per partition"; adding partitions in place; personal data with no erasure path.

CFL-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Identities. clusters (cluster_id, name, region), brokers (cluster_id, broker_id, first_seen_at, decommissioned_at NULL), topics (topic_id UUID, cluster_id, name, created_at, deleted_at NULL), partitions (topic_id, partition_no, created_at). The topic is keyed by its topic id; the name is an attribute, and a recreated topic is a new row with the same name.
  • Facts with validity intervals.
    • broker_attrs (cluster_id, broker_id, rack, host, log_dirs, valid_from, valid_to).
    • topic_configs (topic_id, key, value, valid_from, valid_to).
    • assignments (topic_id, partition_no, replicas int[] in order, adding int[], removing int[], valid_from, valid_to): replica order kept, so replicas[1] is the preferred leader; a reassignment is the interval where adding or removing is non-empty, also summarised in reassignments (topic_id, partition_no, started_at, ended_at, from_replicas, to_replicas).
    • leadership (topic_id, partition_no, leader_broker, leader_epoch, valid_from, valid_to) and isr (topic_id, partition_no, isr int[], valid_from, valid_to): these change most; keep full precision for 30–90 days, then roll up (time under-replicated per partition per day).
    • replica_size_daily (date, topic_id, partition_no, broker_id, log_dir, bytes_max, bytes_end, is_leader_share, rack): the capacity fact, one row per replica per day.
  • Capture. The collector reads the admin interface every {{snapshot_minutes}} minutes, diffs against the last good snapshot and writes change rows (close the old interval at the observation time, open the new one). Each collection writes a collections (cluster_id, collected_at, status ok|partial|failed) row. If a collection fails or returns implausible data (empty replica lists, a broker count drop beyond a threshold), it is marked failed and no changes are written; intervals spanning a gap carry confirmed_until (last ok collection) so a change seen after a gap is known only to have happened within the gap. Consuming the metadata change log directly is a strong alternative where it is exposed.
  • Storage estimate. {{replicas}} replicas × (1440 / {{snapshot_minutes}}) snapshots a day × 395 days: tens of billions to trillions of rows at the larger levels, almost all identical to the previous one. Change intervals are a tiny fraction (assignments change during reassignments; leadership and ISR during incidents and rolls), plus a daily checkpoint per partition to bound as-of lookups.
  • As-of queries. valid_from <= t AND (valid_to > t OR valid_to IS NULL), clustered by (cluster_id, topic_id, valid_from) and with a daily checkpoint table so a query reads at most one day of changes. Rack at the time comes from broker_attrs at t, never from today's broker table.

Competing designs to accept. Full snapshots at a coarse grain (hourly) plus change intervals for leadership and ISR. An event log of metadata changes with projections built on demand. Bitemporal intervals (valid time and recorded time) to show what the system knew when, at Very Hard.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Name as key (recreated topics merged); snapshots every interval forever (storage); empty or partial collections recorded as changes; replica order lost (preferred leader unknown); today's dimensions joined to history; ISR at full precision forever; reassignments invisible (only before and after states).

Incident guidance.

  • Recreated topic summed under one key: rebuild the affected days keyed by topic id and correct the capacity report; guardrail: a uniqueness test on (topic_id) in facts and a check that a name maps to one live topic id at a time.
  • Empty replica lists written during a timeout: delete nothing; mark the collections failed, void the intervals they opened (close them as invalid) and re-derive from the next good snapshot. Guardrail: plausibility checks before diffing (no partition may lose all replicas between two snapshots; replica count drops beyond a threshold mark the collection partial), and alerts read only confirmed state.
  • Audit joined to today's racks: rerun with broker_attrs as of each day; guardrail: placement checks only use interval joins, and the current-state view is not exposed to historical reports.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Interval join of assignments (unnest replicas) to broker_attrs at t, filtered by rack; clustered by topic and time with daily checkpoints. (2) Snapshot rows vs change rows with numbers; keep intervals and daily facts for 13 months, ISR detail for weeks. (3) Two topic ids, two sets of rows; dashboards group by topic id and label by name with the creation date. (4) A failed-collection record, intervals marked unconfirmed for the gap, the reassignment's start or end known only within the gap. (5) leadership intervals vs assignments.replicas[1]; preferred-leader elections show as leadership intervals returning to the first replica.

Rubric anchors. 2: one table of current metadata copied daily, keyed by topic name. 3: identities vs interval facts, topic id key, replica order, a daily capacity fact and a storage estimate. 4: also reassignments explicit, gap handling that never invents changes, rack-at-the-time joins, and ISR retention by grain.

Strong signals. Asks how a recreated topic is identified; treats a missed snapshot as unknown. Red flags. Storing every snapshot for 13 months without estimating it; joining history to current dimensions.

CFL-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Topology.
    1. Source payments (key payment_id, {{partitions}} partitions).
    2. Re-key: selectKey(customer_id); guest payments (null customer id) are branched to a path that emits an enriched record with profile_status = guest and no lookup.
    3. Repartition topic app-payments-by-customer-repartition (delete policy, short retention; the library manages it): key customer id serialised exactly as in customer-profiles, partition count equal to customer-profiles, same partitioner.
    4. Table from customer-profiles (compacted) materialised in a local state store with a changelog topic (compacted). If the source topic is itself compacted and keyed the same way, the library can use it as the changelog instead of creating another copy (an optimisation in Kafka Streams; check current docs).
    5. Left join stream → table: each payment record triggers one output; a profile update does not emit anything. Output to payments-enriched keyed by payment_id again (a second repartition if downstream consumers need payment-id partitioning, or keyed by customer id if fraud scoring is fine with it).
  • Co-partitioning. Same partition count, same key serialisation, same partitioner on both inputs. Different client libraries can use different default partitioners (for example, some non-Java clients default to a different hash; check current docs), so the producer of customer-profiles must be known.
  • Join semantics and missing profiles. Left join with profile_status (found | missing | guest) and the profile's updated_at (or source offset) in the output. A payment arriving before its profile emits missing; optionally, a bounded wait (a small state store of payments without a profile, re-checked when the profile arrives or after N seconds) for fraud models that need the profile, at the cost of latency.
  • Timing. Stream–table joins look up the table's state at processing time; the library aligns inputs by record timestamp on a best-effort basis (configurable idle time). Timestamp-exact lookups need a versioned store, which newer Kafka Streams versions provide (check current docs); without it, reprocessing joins to the table's state as replayed, which is only approximately the state at each payment's event time.
  • Table copied to every instance (GlobalKTable). No repartition and no co-partitioning; but every instance stores all {{profiles}} profiles (tens to hundreds of GB at the larger levels), restores the whole table on start, and lookups are not time-aligned with the stream. Reasonable at Medium, costly at Very Hard.
  • State and restore. Total {{state_gb}} GB spread over instances (for example, 12 instances); restore throughput is bounded by changelog read and local write speed (assume 50–150 MB/s per instance): 60 GB / 12 = 5 GB per instance ≈ 1 minute; 900 GB / 12 = 75 GB ≈ 10–25 minutes. Persistent volumes keep state across restarts (only the tail is restored); one standby replica per task (num.standby.replicas, check current docs) makes failover a promotion instead of a restore.

Competing designs to accept. Flink or ksqlDB with equivalent concepts (keyed state, a changelog or checkpoints, a temporal join against a versioned table). An external key-value store or cache in front of the customer database with a write-through from CDC, if they size the load ({{events_per_sec}} lookups a second), handle slowdowns with timeouts and a missing flag, and accept the loss of time-aligned replay.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Joining without re-keying (wrong partitions, no matches); repartition topic with the wrong partition count or serialiser; inner join (guest and early payments lost); GlobalKTable at hundreds of GB per instance; state on ephemeral disks; no standbys; reprocessing against current profiles (look-ahead bias).

Incident guidance.

  • Key serialisation changed: partition counts matched, so the co-partitioning check passed while keys hashed differently. Roll back the serde; re-emit the affected hour from the source offsets with the correct serde; flag the hour's enriched records as missing-profile in the fraud store. Guardrail: a contract test that serialises a sample key with both producers' serdes and compares bytes and partitions; alert on the missing-profile rate.
  • Full restore from the changelog: move state directories to persistent volumes, add a standby per task, and alert on restore time; estimate restore for the instance's share of {{state_gb}} GB before scaling decisions.
  • Backtest joined to today's profiles: discard the backtest; rebuild with a versioned table (profile as of each payment's event time) or with the profile snapshot recorded in each enriched record at the time, and make that recorded version the only source for training sets.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Source → selectKey → repartition (count = profiles' count) → left join with table (changelog) → output; cleanup policies delete, compact. (2) The library refuses or produces wrong matches; re-key into a repartition topic with the profiles' count, or copy the profiles into a co-partitioned internal topic, or use a global table. (3) Size per instance ÷ restore throughput; standbys make it near zero. (4) Emits missing; fraud scoring sees profile_status and can apply a rule or re-score when the profile arrives. (5) Processing-time lookups and table updates interleave differently on replay; versioned stores or recorded profile versions make it reproducible.

Rubric anchors. 2: joins payments to profiles without re-keying, or calls the database per event with no sizing. 3: repartition topic matched to the table, left join with a missing flag, changelog-backed state, a restore estimate and standbys. 4: also serialiser and partitioner equality, GlobalKTable weighed with numbers, versioned lookups or recorded profile versions for reproducibility, and guest payments handled.
